### 2020

::: {.question-card}
### 2020 May/June · 9231/21 & 9231/22 · Question 2 · 7 marks

It is given that $y=2^x$.

**(a)** By differentiating $\ln y$ with respect to $x$, show that

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=2^x\ln2.
$$

**[3]**

**(b)** Write down $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$. **[1]**

**(c)** Hence find the first three terms in the Maclaurin's series for $2^x$. **[3]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Taking logarithms,

$$
\ln y=x\ln2.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $x$,

$$
\frac1y\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\ln2
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=y\ln2=2^x\ln2.
$$

**(b)**

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=2^x(\ln2)^2}.
$$

**(c)** At $x=0$,

$$
y(0)=1,\qquad y'(0)=\ln2,\qquad y''(0)=(\ln2)^2.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{2^x=1+(\ln2)x+\frac{(\ln2)^2}{2}x^2+\cdots}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2020-mj-21-22-q2"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/21/M/J/2020, Q2; 9231/22/M/J/2020, Q2.</div>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### 2020 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 5(b) · 4 marks

The curve $C$ has parametric equations

$$
x=\frac12t^2-\ln t,\qquad y=2t+1,\qquad \frac12\leqslant t\leqslant2.
$$

Find $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$ in terms of $t$, simplifying your answer.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

$$
\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=t-\frac1t=t-\frac1t,\qquad
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=2.
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac2{t-\frac1t}=\frac{2t}{t^2-1}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t$,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right)
=\frac{2(t^2-1)-2t(2t)}{(t^2-1)^2}
=-\frac{2(t^2+1)}{(t^2-1)^2}.
$$

Applying the chain rule,

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}
=-\frac{2(1+t^{-2})}{(t-t^{-1})^3}
=-\frac{2t(t^2+1)}{(t^2-1)^3}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2020-mj-23-q5b"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/23/M/J/2020, Q5(b).</div>
:::

### 2020 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 6(b)–(c) · 9 marks

The variables $x$ and $y$ are such that

$$
\tanh y=\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),
\qquad -\frac{\pi}{4}\leqslant x\leqslant\frac{3\pi}{4}.
$$

**(b)** By differentiating the equation $\tanh y=\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ with respect to $x$, show that

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\operatorname{cosec}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right).
$$

**[4]**

**(c)** Hence find the first three terms in the Maclaurin's series for

$$
\tanh^{-1}\left(\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)
$$

in the form

$$
\frac12\ln a+bx+cx^2,
$$

giving the exact values of the constants $a$, $b$ and $c$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(b)** Differentiating $\tanh y=\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$,

$$
\operatorname{sech}^2y\,\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}
=-\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right).
$$

Using $1-\tanh^2y=\operatorname{sech}^2y$,

$$
\left(1-\cos^2\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}
=-\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right).
$$

Therefore

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}
=-\frac{\sin\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}{\sin^2\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}
=\boxed{-\operatorname{cosec}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)}.
$$

**(c)** Let $y=\tanh^{-1}\left(\cos\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right)$. At $x=0$,

$$
y(0)=\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)=\frac12\ln\left(\frac{2+\sqrt2}{2-\sqrt2}\right)=\frac12\ln(3+2\sqrt2).
$$

From part (b),

$$
y'(0)=-\operatorname{cosec}\frac{\pi}{4}=-\sqrt2.
$$

Differentiating $y'=-\operatorname{cosec}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$,

$$
y''(x)=\operatorname{cosec}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\cot\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),
$$

so

$$
y''(0)=\sqrt2.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{y=\frac12\ln(3+2\sqrt2)-\sqrt2\,x+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}x^2}.
$$

So $a=3+2\sqrt2$, $b=-\sqrt2$ and $c=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}$.

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2020-mj-23-q6bc"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/23/M/J/2020, Q6(b)–(c).</div>
:::

::: {.question-card}
### 2020 October/November · 9231/21 & 9231/23 · Question 5 · 9 marks

It is given that

$$
x=\sinh^{-1}t,\qquad y=\cos^{-1}t,\qquad -1\leqslant t\leqslant1.
$$

**(a)** By differentiating $\cos y$ with respect to $t$, show that

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=-\frac1{\sqrt{1-t^2}}.
$$

**[4]**

**(b)** Find $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$ in terms of $t$, simplifying your answer. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** From $y=\cos^{-1}t$ we have $\cos y=t$. Differentiating with respect to $t$,

$$
-\sin y\,\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=1.
$$

Since $0<y<\pi$, $\sin y>0$, so

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=-\frac1{\sin y}
=-\frac1{\sqrt{1-\cos^2y}}
=\boxed{-\frac1{\sqrt{1-t^2}}}.
$$

**(b)** Since $x=\sinh^{-1}t$,

$$
\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=\frac1{\sqrt{1+t^2}}.
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}
=-\frac{\sqrt{1+t^2}}{\sqrt{1-t^2}}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t$ and applying the chain rule,

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}
=-\frac{2t}{(1-t^2)^{3/2}}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2020-on-21-23-q5"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Sources:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/21/O/N/2020, Q5; 9231/23/O/N/2020, Q5.</div>
:::

### 2020 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 1 · 5 marks

Find the Maclaurin's series for $\tan\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$ up to and including the term in $x^2$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Let $f(x)=\tan\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)$. Then

$$
f(0)=1,
$$

$$
f'(x)=\sec^2\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),
\qquad
f'(0)=\sec^2\frac{\pi}{4}=2,
$$

$$
f''(x)=2\sec^2\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\tan\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right),
\qquad
f''(0)=2(2)(1)=4.
$$

Hence

$$
\boxed{\tan\left(x+\frac{\pi}{4}\right)=1+2x+2x^2+\cdots}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2020-on-22-q1"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/22/O/N/2020, Q1.</div>
:::

### 2021

::: {.question-card}
### 2021 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 2 · 7 marks

Find the Maclaurin's series for $\ln\cosh x$ up to and including the term in $x^4$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Let $f(x)=\ln\cosh x$. Then

$$
f(0)=0,\qquad
f'(x)=\tanh x,
\qquad
f''(x)=\operatorname{sech}^2x,
$$

$$
f'''(x)=-2\operatorname{sech}^2x\tanh x=-2\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh^3x},
$$

$$
f^{(4)}(x)=-2\frac{\cosh^2x-3\sinh^2x}{\cosh^4x}.
$$

At $x=0$,

$$
f(0)=0,\quad f'(0)=0,\quad f''(0)=1,\quad f'''(0)=0,\quad f^{(4)}(0)=-2.
$$

Therefore

$$
\boxed{\ln\cosh x=\frac12x^2-\frac1{12}x^4+\cdots}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2021-mj-23-q2"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/23/M/J/2021, Q2.</div>
:::

### 2021 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 1 · 3 marks

It is given that $y=\sinh(x^2)+\cosh(x^2)$.

**(a)** Use standard results from the list of formulae (MF19) to find the Maclaurin's series for $y$ in terms of $x$ up to and including the term in $x^4$. **[2]**

**(b)** Deduce the value of $\dfrac{\mathrm d^4y}{\mathrm dx^4}$ when $x=0$. **[1]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Since

$$
e^{x^2}=\cosh(x^2)+\sinh(x^2),
$$

the Maclaurin series is

$$
\boxed{y=e^{x^2}=1+x^2+\frac12x^4+\cdots}.
$$

**(b)** The coefficient of $x^4$ is $\dfrac{1}{4!}\dfrac{\mathrm d^4y}{\mathrm dx^4}(0)=\dfrac12$, so

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^4y}{\mathrm dx^4}(0)=12}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2021-on-22-q1"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/22/O/N/2021, Q1.</div>

### 2021 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 5(b) · 4 marks

The curve $C$ has parametric equations

$$
x=3t+2t^{-1}+at^3,\qquad y=4t-\frac32t^{-1}+bt^3,\qquad 1\leqslant t\leqslant2,
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are constants.

It is given instead that $a=b=0$. Find the value of $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$ when $t=1$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

With $a=b=0$,

$$
x=3t+2t^{-1},\qquad y=4t-\frac32t^{-1}.
$$

Then

$$
\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=3-2t^{-2},\qquad
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=4+\frac32t^{-2},
$$

so

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{4+\frac32t^{-2}}{3-2t^{-2}}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t$,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right)
=\frac{(3-2t^{-2})(-3t^{-3})-(4+\frac32t^{-2})(4t^{-3})}{(3-2t^{-2})^2}
=-\frac{25t^{-3}}{(3-2t^{-2})^2}.
$$

Applying the chain rule with $\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=3-2t^{-2}$,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}
=-\frac{25t^{-3}}{(3-2t^{-2})^3}.
$$

At $t=1$,

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=-25}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2021-on-22-q5b"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/22/O/N/2021, Q5(b).</div>
:::

### 2022 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 2(a) · 4 marks

Find the coefficient of $x^2$ in the Maclaurin's series for $-\ln\cos x$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Let $f(x)=-\ln\cos x$. Then

$$
f'(x)=\tan x,\qquad f''(x)=\sec^2x.
$$

At $x=0$,

$$
f'(0)=0,\qquad f''(0)=1.
$$

Hence the coefficient of $x^2$ is

$$
\boxed{\frac{f''(0)}{2!}=\frac12}.
$$

</details>

### 2022 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 4 · 9 marks

It is given that

$$
x=-t+\tan^{-1}t,\qquad y=t+\sinh^{-1}t.
$$

**(a)** Show that

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\frac{\sqrt{1+t^2}+1+t^2}{t^2}.
$$

**[4]**

**(b)** Find the value of $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$ when $t=\frac34$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)**

$$
\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=-1+\frac1{1+t^2}=-\frac{t^2}{1+t^2},
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=1+\frac1{\sqrt{1+t^2}}.
$$

Therefore

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}
=\frac{1+\frac1{\sqrt{1+t^2}}}{-\frac{t^2}{1+t^2}}
=-\frac{(1+t^2)\left(1+\frac1{\sqrt{1+t^2}}\right)}{t^2}
=-\frac{1+t^2+\sqrt{1+t^2}}{t^2}.
$$

So

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\frac{\sqrt{1+t^2}+1+t^2}{t^2}}.
$$

**(b)** Differentiating $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right)
=-\frac{t^2\left(2t+\frac{t}{\sqrt{1+t^2}}\right)-2t\left(1+t^2+\sqrt{1+t^2}\right)}{t^4}.
$$

Applying the chain rule,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}
=\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right)\cdot\frac{\mathrm dt}{\mathrm dx}
=-\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}\right)\cdot\frac{1+t^2}{t^2}.
$$

At $t=\frac34$ this simplifies to

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=-\frac{80}{3}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2022-mj-23-q4"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/23/M/J/2022, Q4.</div>
:::

### 2023 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 1 · 5 marks

Find the Maclaurin's series for $\ln(x+2)+\ln(x^2+5)$ up to and including the term in $x^2$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Using $\ln(1+u)=u-\frac12u^2+\cdots$,

$$
\ln(x+2)=\ln2+\ln\left(1+\frac{x}{2}\right)
=\ln2+\frac{x}{2}-\frac{x^2}{8}+\cdots,
$$

$$
\ln(x^2+5)=\ln5+\ln\left(1+\frac{x^2}{5}\right)
=\ln5+\frac{x^2}{5}+\cdots.
$$

Adding,

$$
\boxed{\ln(x+2)+\ln(x^2+5)=\ln10+\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3x^2}{40}+\cdots}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2023-on-22-q1"> Completed</label>

### 2023 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 2(b) · 4 marks

The curve $C$ has parametric equations

$$
x=e^{-t}(t^3+t^2),\qquad y=2e^t(t-1),\qquad 0\leqslant t\leqslant1.
$$

Find $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$ in terms of $t$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

$$
\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=e^{-t}(-t^3-t^2+3t^2+2t)=e^{-t}(-t^3+2t^2+2t),
$$

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=2e^t(t-1)+2e^t=2te^t.
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{2te^t}{e^{-t}(-t^3+2t^2+2t)}
=\frac{2te^{2t}}{-t^3+2t^2+2t}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t$ and applying the chain rule,

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=t^3e^t(t^2+4t+2)}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2023-on-22-q2b"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/22/O/N/2023, Q2(b).</div>
:::

### 2024 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 2(b) · 5 marks

The curve $C$ has parametric equations

$$
x=\cosh t,\qquad y=\sinh t,\qquad 0\leqslant t\leqslant\frac35.
$$

The length of $C$ is denoted by $s$.

**(a)** Show that $s=\displaystyle\int_0^{3/5}\sqrt{\cosh 2t}\,\mathrm dt$. **[4]**

**(b)** By finding the Maclaurin's series for $\sqrt{\cosh 2t}$ up to and including the term in $t^2$, deduce an approximation to $s$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Differentiating,

$$
\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=\sinh t,\qquad
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=\cosh t.
$$

Therefore

$$
\left(\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}\right)^2+\left(\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}\right)^2
=\sinh^2t+\cosh^2t=\cosh 2t,
$$

so

$$
s=\int_0^{3/5}\sqrt{\cosh 2t}\,\mathrm dt.
$$

**(b)** Using $\sqrt{\cosh 2t}\approx1+t^2$ (from the Maclaurin series of $\cosh 2t$ up to $t^2$),

$$
s\approx\int_0^{3/5}(1+t^2)\,\mathrm dt
=\left[t+\frac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^{3/5}
=\frac35+\frac{9}{125}
=\boxed{\frac{84}{125}=0.672}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2024-mj-23-q2b"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/23/M/J/2024, Q2(b).</div>
:::

### 2024 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 3(b) · 5 marks

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
3x^2+2xy+24y^2=13.
$$

**(a)** Show that, at the point $(-2,-1)$ on $C$, $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\dfrac12$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find the value of $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$ at the point $(-2,-1)$. **[5]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Differentiating implicitly,

$$
6x+2xy'+2y+48yy'=0.
$$

At $(-2,-1)$,

$$
3(-2)^2+2(-2)y'+2(-1)+24(-1)^2y'=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
12-4y'-2+24y'=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
20y'=-10
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\boxed{y'=-\frac12}.
$$

**(b)** Differentiating

$$
3x^2+2xy'+2y+24y^2y'=0
$$

with respect to $x$,

$$
6x+2xy''+2y'+2y'+24y^2y''+48y(y')^2=0.
$$

Substituting $x=-2$, $y=-1$ and $y'=-\frac12$,

$$
6(-2)+2(-2)y''+4\left(-\frac12\right)+24(-1)^2y''+48(-1)\left(-\frac12\right)^2=0.
$$

That is,

$$
-12-4y''-2+24y''-12=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
20y''-26=0,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{13}{10}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2024-mj-23-q3b"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/23/M/J/2024, Q3(b).</div>
:::

### 2024 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 7(a) · 3 marks

Show that

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{x^2-9}-\frac{9}{2}\cosh^{-1}\frac{x}{3}\right)=\sqrt{x^2-9}.
$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Using the product rule and $\dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\cosh^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3}=\dfrac1{\sqrt{x^2-9}}$,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{x^2-9}\right)
=\frac12\sqrt{x^2-9}+\frac{x^2}{2\sqrt{x^2-9}},
$$

and

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(-\frac92\cosh^{-1}\frac{x}{3}\right)
=-\frac92\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{x^2-9}}.
$$

Adding,

$$
\frac12\sqrt{x^2-9}+\frac{x^2-9}{2\sqrt{x^2-9}}
=\frac12\sqrt{x^2-9}+\frac12\sqrt{x^2-9}
=\sqrt{x^2-9}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2024-mj-23-q7a"> Completed</label>

### 2024 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 2 · 7 marks

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
4y^2+4\ln(xy)=1.
$$

**(a)** Show that, at the point $\left(2,\frac12\right)$ on $C$, $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\dfrac16$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find the value of $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$ at the point $\left(2,\frac12\right)$. **[4]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Differentiating implicitly,

$$
8yy'+4\cdot\frac{xy'+y}{xy}=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
8yy'+4y^{-1}y'+4x^{-1}=0.
$$

At $\left(2,\frac12\right)$,

$$
8\left(\frac12\right)y'+4(2)y'+\frac42=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
4y'+8y'+2=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
y'=-\frac16.
$$

**(b)** Differentiating again,

$$
8(y')^2+8yy''-4(y')^2y^{-2}+4y^{-1}y''-4x^{-2}=0.
$$

Substituting $x=2$, $y=\frac12$ and $y'=-\frac16$,

$$
8\cdot\frac1{36}+4y''-4\cdot\frac1{36}\cdot4+8y''-1=0.
$$

Solving gives

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{11}{108}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="diff-p2-2024-on-22-q2"> Completed</label>
<div class="source-line"><strong>Source:</strong> Cambridge International 9231/22/O/N/2024, Q2.</div>
:::

### 2024 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 7(a) · 3 marks

Show that

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(\ln\tanh x\right)=2\operatorname{cosech}2x.
$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Using the chain rule,

$$
\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\left(\ln\tanh x\right)
=\frac{\operatorname{sech}^2x}{\tanh x}
=\frac1{\sinh x\cosh x}
=\frac2{\sinh2x}
=\boxed{2\operatorname{cosech}2x}.
$$

</details>

### 2025 May/June · 9231/23 · Question 3 · 10 marks

The curve $C$ has equation

$$
9y^2-3\sinh^{-1}(xy)=1-3\ln3.
$$

**(a)** Show that, at the point $(4,\frac13)$ on $C$, $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=-\dfrac12$. **[4]**

**(b)** Find the value of $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$ at the point $(4,\frac13)$. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Differentiating implicitly,

$$
18yy'-3\cdot\frac{xy'+y}{\sqrt{1+x^2y^2}}=0.
$$

At $(4,\frac13)$,

$$
18\cdot\frac13\,y'-3\cdot\frac{4y'+\frac13}{\sqrt{1+\frac{16}9}}=0.
$$

Since $\sqrt{1+\frac{16}9}=\frac53$,

$$
6y'-3\cdot\frac{4y'+\frac13}{\frac53}=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
6y'-\frac95\left(4y'+\frac13\right)=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
6y'-\frac{36}{5}y'-\frac35=0.
$$

Multiplying through by $5$,

$$
30y'-36y'-3=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
-6y'=3
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\boxed{y'=-\frac12}.
$$

**(b)** Differentiating

$$
18yy'-\frac{3(xy'+y)}{\sqrt{1+x^2y^2}}=0
$$

with respect to $x$ gives

$$
18yy''+18(y')^2
-3\cdot\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2y^2}(xy''+2y')-(xy'+y)\cdot\frac{x^2y}{\sqrt{1+x^2y^2}}}{1+x^2y^2}=0.
$$

Substituting $x=4$, $y=\frac13$, $y'=-\frac12$ gives

$$
-6y''+\frac{87}{10}=0,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{29}{4}}.
$$

</details>

### 2025 October/November · 9231/22 · Question 3 · 9 marks

The variables $x$ and $y$ are such that $y=2$ when $x=-1$ and

$$
x^2y+(x+y)^3=3.
$$

**(a)** Show that $\dfrac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\dfrac14$ when $x=-1$. **[3]**

**(b)** Find the value of $\dfrac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}$ when $x=-1$. **[6]**

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

**(a)** Differentiating implicitly,

$$
x^2y'+2xy+3(x+y)^2(1+y')=0.
$$

At $(-1,2)$,

$$
y'+2(-1)(2)+3(1)^2(1+y')=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
y'-4+3+3y'=0
\;\Longrightarrow\;
4y'=1
\;\Longrightarrow\;
\boxed{y'=\frac14}.
$$

**(b)** Differentiating again,

$$
x^2y''+4xy'+2y+3(x+y)^2y''+6(1+y')^2(x+y)=0.
$$

Substituting $x=-1$, $y=2$, $y'=\frac14$,

$$
y''-1+4+3y''+6\left(\frac54\right)^2(1)=0.
$$

Solving gives

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=-\frac{99}{32}}.
$$

</details>

### 2025 October/November · 9231/24 · Question 7(b) · 5 marks

The curve $C$ has parametric equations

$$
x=8\ln\left(\tan\frac{t}{2}\right)-3\cot t-3t,\qquad
y=6\ln\left(\tan\frac{t}{2}\right)+4\cot t+4t,
$$

for $\frac{\pi}{6}\leqslant t\leqslant\frac{\pi}{3}$.

Show that

$$
\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}=\frac{a\cot t\operatorname{cosec}t(\operatorname{cosec}^2t+1)}{(b\operatorname{cosec}t+c\cot^2t)^n},
$$

where $a$, $b$, $c$ and $n$ are integers to be determined.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show answer and mark scheme</summary>

Differentiating,

$$
\frac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}=8\operatorname{cosec}t+3\cot^2t,
\qquad
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dt}=6\operatorname{cosec}t-4\cot^2t.
$$

Hence

$$
\frac{\mathrm dy}{\mathrm dx}=\frac{6\operatorname{cosec}t-4\cot^2t}{8\operatorname{cosec}t+3\cot^2t}.
$$

Differentiating this with respect to $t$ and applying the chain rule gives

$$
\boxed{\frac{\mathrm d^2y}{\mathrm dx^2}
=\frac{50\cot t\operatorname{cosec}t(\operatorname{cosec}^2t+1)}{(8\operatorname{cosec}t+3\cot^2t)^3}}.
$$

So $a=50$, $b=8$, $c=3$ and $n=3$.

</details>
